Something you're quick to realize when you work in healthcare is that everyone shits, everyone pees and everyone pukes. There's a lot of nasty body things going on, but that's okay. It's natural. We're actually worried if you don't pee or poop. In fact, we're so worried that we'll give you something to fix that. Bodily fluids happen.

Some people need help getting on the loo, some people just need their diaper changed while standing up, and some people are bedridden and need help in bed. It's icky, but it's work. You do what you have to. You usually do this work alone. You're two or more if the nurse/caregiver is new, the patient is being difficult or.. if the patient is fat. Or if you have to use a lift to move the person, but you can be alone as soon as the person is back in the bed/chair/wherever.

Why do you need to be two to if it's someone fat? Size and weight.

Weight.

You can deal with a lot of weight when you're dealing with a person who's bedridden. We have moving techniques, and with the help of a silky blanket we can move around a person pretty easily. There's also a "momentum" type of thing ,where you use the body's shape and natural movements to move someone. I can roll around full grown (and tall!) people like marbles. So if someone needs assistance in moving a person around that person is heavy. There's only so much a person can roll around. But the biggest issue that makes it impossible to deal with, is size.

.

Body size.

When you move a person around in bed using their body you're generally pushing on their bones. You bend their knee and push on the knee+hip/back to make them roll to the side. A person can be chubby, no worries. It's still possible to push that person around.

It is not, however, that easy to push a hammy around. Instead of pushing at bones your hands dig into their flesh like a fatty digs into cake. There's no leverage. There's just flesh, flesh and more flesh that gets pushed aside. "But Alpaca, just keep on pushing it aside, you'll reach bone soon enough!"

I freaking wish.

You need two hands (at least) to push at the flesh in one place. You can't roll a person around by just pushing on their leg. You need to push on their back as well (unless you feel like breaking their hip, that's cool too). But both of the hands are busy trying to get a good grip on the leg, so there's no arm left to push on the back. Thus, you need someone to grab the fatty from the other side of the bed and lasso that person to their side like a cattle. No, seriously, I've worked at a farm. Like a cattle.

"That doesn't sound too bad though! Work is done!"

Wrong.

We don't move around people like this because it's fun. It's usually because 1) they need to be shifted every once in a while 2) they need a change of clothes/sheets or 3) They need a wash or a diaperchange. Number 3 happens often.

So, you've got two people pushing and moving this blobby bag around. You've got no real grip on the person since everything's soft, so your hands just slide around or (if you're unlucky) inside a fold. Yeah. That's fun. Very.. very.. fun. And while these people are holding this ham , they also have to remove the diaper, clean the person and put in another diaper.

Now, normally, this is pretty simple. You hold the person up with one hand, and use the other to wipe/bathe. You then put a new diaper slightly beneath/behind them, roll them around and pull it out from the other side. What's the difference when it comes to a fat person?

Folds. Flesh. Skin. If you're lucky you'll have a third person who can hold the folds up for you. If you're unlucky (and you usually are, cause there's seriously not enough staffing at my job) the folds on your side will flop around. A cleaned fold that flops against a dirty fold will get dirty. You have to rewipe. A lot. You go through a freaking rainforest everytime you clean a fatty. And once you think you're done, you check another area, or under another fold and tadaaa.. more poop. It's the shittiest treasurehunt in the universe.

But you clean that, curse, cry, try to squish the diaper under the body (which is hard, cause a lot of times you just end up pushing it beneath a fold) and then you turn it around. It's the same freaking party all over again. And once that person is rolled over you notice that the folds that were against the bed before also contain poop. Yay! But none of that can compare to the..

.

Smell and wounds.

Chub rub/pressure wounds. We joke about it, but in old or sick people who can't move around a lot it happens (or something that's very similar). Usually in thighs, armpits or beneath the boobs on old ladies. Sometimes it happens in feet if they've been lying against a surface for too long, or to backs and buts. It's uncomfortable, and pretty sad. I wish I could fix it but all I can do is to massage the area to make the blood flow, and to try and air it out as much as possible.

In fatties, it happens beneath folds. All of them. And they sweat. And sometimes they get poop or food in the folds. It smells from far away. It's uncomfortable for them. It itches. It oozes. In most cases, it's actually more like fold mold than chub rub.

Now imagine standing a few inches from them while you're cleaning their folds from various body fluids. It's awful. And it's a lot, mainly because the folds are big. They go in deep in some patients, so there's a lot of place for stuff to grow. Damp, warm, dark, sweaty. It's a freaking party for bacteria. And don't get me started on beetus feet. Beetus feet and fold mold smell equally bad. It's a sickingly sweet smell and it gets stuck to the roof of your mouth. It's also very thick. I imagine it smells like what a stew from hell would smell like.

.
